name: Rickettsial Diseases
aliases: Spotted fever and typhus group infections

clinicalPearls: Rickettsiae are small, obligately intracellular, gram-negative coccobacilli/short bacilli, most spread by a tick, mite, flea, or louse; except for louse-borne typhus, humans are incidental hosts. The agents span seven genera (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Neorickettsia, Candidatus Neoehrlichia, and Coxiella).

During the first roughly 5 days the acute presentations are largely indistinguishable: fever, headache, and myalgia, with or without nausea, vomiting, and cough; later differentiating features such as rash, eschar, pneumonitis, or meningoencephalitis emerge. Heightened clinical suspicion based on exposure history should prompt empiric antibiotics rather than waiting for confirmation (p.1454).

A characteristic laboratory triad supports the diagnosis across many of these infections: thrombocytopenia, a normal or low white-cell count, mildly to moderately elevated hepatic aminotransferases, and hyponatremia (p.1454).

Coxiella burnetii, R. prowazekii, and R. typhi can survive long periods outside the host and are highly infectious by inhalation (a single Coxiella organism can cause pneumonia), making several agents bioterrorism concerns (p.1454).

In Rocky Mountain spotted fever the rash is progressive and unreliable: present in only about 14% on day 1 and roughly 49% by day 3, appearing on day 6 or later in ~20% and never appearing in about 10% of cases; classic palm/sole involvement tends to come late and may not occur at all (p.1456-1457).

Only about 3% of RMSF patients show the classic triad of fever, rash, and tick exposure in the first 3 days, and only ~60% recall a tick bite; serology is typically negative at presentation, so treatment must not await a positive result (p.1457).

An eschar (tache noire) at the bite site is a useful clue in several spotted fevers (notably African tick-bite fever ~90%, rickettsialpox, Mediterranean spotted fever ~50%) and in scrub typhus, but is absent in the typhus group (epidemic and murine typhus have no eschar) (p.1455).

Ehrlichioses/anaplasmoses (Anaplasmataceae) target hematopoietic cells: E. chaffeensis (HME) and E. muris infect mononuclear phagocytes, while E. ewingii and A. phagocytophilum (HGA) infect neutrophils; intracytoplasmic morulae may be seen on blood smear but only in a minority (about 20% or less in HME, 20-75% in HGA) (p.1460-1462).

Of the Rickettsiaceae, in descending case-fatality order the life-threatening species are R. rickettsii (RMSF), R. prowazekii (louse-borne typhus), Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus), R. conorii (MSF), and R. typhi (murine typhus); many spotted-fever species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never been documented to cause a fatal illness (p.1456).

Of the rickettsial agents, only C. burnetii is documented to cause chronic illness, and only R. prowazekii causes a recrudescent illness (Brill-Zinsser disease) when latent infection reactivates years after the acute episode (p.1454, p.1459).

Q fever is an inhalational zoonosis from sheep, goats, and cattle (organism shed heavily in parturition material); the infectious dose is extremely low (probably 1-10 organisms) and ~60% of infections are asymptomatic seroconversions. Acute disease presents geographically as either pneumonia or hepatitis (p.1462).

Scrub typhus shows remarkable antigenic diversity with rapid loss of cross-protective immunity, so reinfection can occur within weeks to months; the classic eschar/rash/lymphadenopathy triad is often absent, with under half of travelers developing an eschar and under 40% a rash (p.1460).
harrison.pathophysiology: The spotted fever and typhus group organisms (Rickettsia and Orientia) infect vascular endothelial cells and disseminate lymphohematogenously, producing widespread small-vessel infection. The fundamental injury is increased vascular permeability rather than occlusive thrombosis or ischemic necrosis; resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia drive the clinical picture. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in roughly a third to half of RMSF cases, but overt DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; thrombin generation and fibrinolysis appear to be homeostatic responses to nonocclusive hemostatic plugs at sites of endothelial injury. Hyponatremia reflects appropriate ADH secretion in response to hypovolemia. Pathogenic rickettsiae have small, reductively evolved genomes lacking biosynthetic genes for intracellularly available molecules. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma instead parasitize vacuoles of hematopoietic cells; vasculitis and granulomas are not features of HME or HGA. Coxiella burnetii is genetically distinct from the Rickettsiaceae, survives harsh environments, escapes macrophage killing by inhibiting the final step of phagosome maturation, and adapts to the acidic phagolysosome.
additionalDifferentials: Influenza and other viral febrile illnesses
Gram-negative or gram-positive bacterial sepsis / toxic shock syndrome
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Bacterial or viral meningoencephalitis (when CNS involvement predominates)
Acute abdomen / enterocolitis (when GI symptoms predominate, has prompted laparotomy)
infectionMimics: Other rickettsioses within the group (RMSF vs HME, HGA, murine typhus, sylvatic flying-squirrel typhus, rickettsialpox can mimic one another)
Epidemic typhus is frequently misdiagnosed as typhoid fever in tropical settings
HGA can mimic atypical or severe Lyme disease and patients may develop Lyme antibodies without true co-infection
Leptospirosis, dengue, and other tropical febrile illnesses
Q fever pneumonia mimics community-acquired pneumonia of other etiologies; Q fever hepatitis mimics other granulomatous hepatitides
nonInfectiousMimics: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Acute abdomen prompting exploratory laparotomy when abdominal pain and tenderness dominate
additionalInvestigations: Indirect immunofluorescence (IFA) serology on paired acute and convalescent sera is the mainstay; for RMSF a titer of >=64 is not detectable until ~7-10 days after onset (IgG sensitivity 89-100%, specificity 99-100%), so it is usually negative at presentation
Immunohistologic (immunohistochemical) examination of a 3-mm punch biopsy of a rash lesion for R. rickettsii is ~70% sensitive and 100% specific - the most useful test during acute RMSF

PCR on skin/eschar biopsy or swab (higher yield than blood); PCR of peripheral blood is generally insufficiently sensitive for RMSF and typhus because organisms are concentrated in endothelium, not circulation
Peripheral-blood smear for intracytoplasmic morulae (ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis); cell-culture isolation is feasible but rarely done due to technical difficulty and biohazard

For Q fever, IFA is the serologic gold standard distinguishing acute (phase II IgG seroconversion, fourfold rise) from chronic disease (high phase I IgG, e.g. titer >512 or >=1:800/1:1024); ELISA and complement fixation are alternatives; PCR on blood/serum can be positive in the first 1-2 weeks

For chronic Q fever, imaging including transesophageal echocardiography (higher vegetation detection than transthoracic) and FDG-PET/CT to detect valvular, intravascular, osteomyelitic, or lymphadenitic foci

Supportive labs: CBC (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia/neutropenia), hepatic aminotransferases, serum sodium, acute-phase proteins (CRP, procalcitonin, ferritin, fibrinogen), creatine kinase in suspected myositis; CSF analysis when meningoencephalitis is suspected
redFlags: Petechial or hemorrhagic rash, especially with palm/sole involvement, in a febrile patient with possible tick exposure (advanced RMSF)
Progressive worsening over days after an initial viral-seeming presentation - mandates re-evaluation, as RMSF mimics viral illness early
Altered mental status, confusion, lethargy, stupor, ataxia, seizures, or coma (meningoencephalitis)
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, ARDS, or need for mechanical ventilation
Hypotension, sepsis/septic-shock-like or toxic-shock-like presentation with multiorgan failure
Fulminant RMSF (death within 5 days), seen most often in Black male patients with G6PD deficiency
Acute kidney injury / oliguria, jaundice, gastrointestinal bleeding (hematemesis/melena)
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or a DIC-like picture in ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis
Immunocompromise (diabetes, cancer, transplant, asplenia, hepatitis C, HIV, immunosuppressive drugs) markedly raises risk of severe/fatal ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis
Culture-negative endocarditis, infected aneurysm, or infected vascular prosthesis suggesting chronic Q fever
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on early recognition and prompt empiric therapy. RMSF mortality was 20-25% before antibiotics and is roughly 3-5% now, principally driven by diagnostic/treatment delay; confirmed-case fatality is higher (~9-10% in regions where R. rickettsii is the sole spotted-fever species), is highest in children under 10 and adults over 70, and approaches 50% in parts of Mexico and Brazil for unknown reasons. Untreated fatal RMSF typically dies 8-15 days after onset. Survivors usually recover fully, but severe disease can leave permanent neurologic deficits or gangrene requiring amputation. Mediterranean spotted fever has a severe form (~50% mortality) in patients with diabetes, alcoholism, or heart failure. Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus is fatal in 7-40% of untreated cases. Untreated classic scrub typhus has ~6% case-fatality. Acute Q fever case-fatality is ~1-2%; chronic Q fever carries high mortality (~25% in proven Dutch-outbreak cases, highest at 33% when both endocarditis and vascular infection are present). Q fever fatigue syndrome follows up to 20% of acute cases. Many SFG species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never caused documented fatal illness, and African tick-bite fever is typically mild.
pitfalls: Waiting for serologic confirmation before treating - serology is usually negative at acute presentation; delay worsens outcome and empiric doxycycline should not be withheld
Excluding RMSF because there is no rash or no recalled tick bite (~10% never rash; only ~60% recall a bite) or because palms/soles are not involved

Interpreting a single acute-phase positive titer as diagnostic in endemic areas - cross-reactive preexisting antibody (e.g., from the highly prevalent R. amblyommatis or in HGA-endemic regions) can mislead; the recent apparent RMSF surge largely reflects cross-reactive single-titer enzyme immunoassays rather than true R. rickettsii disease
Relying on blood PCR for RMSF or typhus - insufficiently sensitive because organisms reside in endothelium, not blood; skin/eschar biopsy is preferable
Assuming negative HME serology because E. chaffeensis tests can cross-react when the true agent is another Ehrlichia; separate specific tests are needed for HME vs HGA

Overlooking chronic Q fever as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis or unexplained infected aneurysm/vascular prosthesis - median latency from primary infection is ~13 months and can exceed 9 years
Mislabeling epidemic typhus as typhoid fever in tropical/resource-limited settings
Attributing prolonged post-Q-fever fatigue to active infection and prescribing antibiotics - a randomized trial showed long-term doxycycline did not reduce fatigue versus placebo
harrison.severityClassification: No single unified rickettsial severity score; severity is judged by organ-system involvement and progression. Across the group, escalating clinical lines after nonspecific fever are: (1) macular/maculopapular rash; (2) eschar at the bite site; (3) vesicular rash; (4) pneumonitis with radiographic opacities/rales; (5) meningoencephalitis; and (6) progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (sepsis/toxic-shock-like). For Q fever, the Dutch consensus group classifies chronic disease as proven, probable, or possible based on PCR positivity in blood/tissue or phase I IgG IFA >=1:800/1:1024 combined with endocarditis (modified Duke criteria), proven large-vessel/prosthetic infection on imaging, or compatible clinical and histologic findings.
management: Give empirical doxycycline of the tetracycline class promptly on clinical and epidemiological suspicion, without waiting for serological confirmation, as the mainstay across spotted-fever, typhus and ehrlichial or anaplasmal infections
Use chloramphenicol only as an alternative in specific circumstances, since doxycycline remains preferred even in children and pregnancy for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
Treat Q fever with doxycycline, adding hydroxychloroquine for chronic endocarditic or endovascular disease
Provide supportive care for the increased vascular permeability with judicious fluid resuscitation and organ support in severe disease
Monitor for and manage complications including encephalitis, respiratory failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation and renal impairment
Advise vector avoidance, protective clothing and prompt tick removal
Notify public-health authorities and pursue echocardiographic and imaging surveillance for chronic Q-fever endovascular foci
